objection: The page said the median was 7 days everywhere, but Federal Shipping and very large orders have a median of 6 days.
resolution: Confirmed and corrected: the page now says 6–7 days.

claim: Q3: 97% of late dispatches are slow orders
objection: This is close to automatic: any late order with a 28-day window took more than 28 days, so it is slow by definition.
resolution: Confirmed; the claim was removed. The late rate for 14-day orders is reported instead, with its 95% range.

claim: Q3: carriers dispatch 1.3 and 1.8 days slower
objection: The gap comes entirely from the slowest 10% of orders, and 'carriers dispatch slower' implies a cause the data can't show.
resolution: Confirmed: without the slowest orders the gaps are 0.4 and 0.2 days and not material. The page now says these carriers' shipments are more often among the very slow orders (13% and 9% vs 6%), that the data doesn't show why, and the regression without slow orders is in this appendix.

claim: Q3: freight differences not material, so renegotiating isn't supported
objection: The intervals are wide (about −5% to +34%), so the honest result is inconclusive rather than 'no difference'.
resolution: Accepted: the page now calls the freight comparison inconclusive and gives the range.

objection: A higher late rate follows partly from a shorter window; the real evidence is that their median processing time is no faster. The sample is small.
resolution: Accepted: the median comparison (7.5 vs 7 days) now comes first, with the 95% range of 10–28%.

objection: Dependence is measured over a different window from growth. Over the compared periods, QUICK-Stop is 50% and Hungry Owl 43%, below the 50% line.
resolution: Confirmed. The approved rule (latest four quarters) is kept, but the page now gives both figures and calls Germany's and UK & Ireland's concentration borderline.

objection: Directions depend on the quarters compared; Brazil, UK & Ireland and the Nordics flip.
resolution: Confirmed with a new three-period check (in this appendix). The key finding now names only the markets that move the same way in all three, and actions for the others are marked tentative.

objection: Brazil is 'not conclusive' in the bootstrap check, its direction flips, and 76% of its gain is one customer.
resolution: Confirmed; the action is now marked tentative, with the reason given.

objection: The figure depends heavily on which quarters are compared.
resolution: Accepted: the page gives the range (+42% to +116%).

objection: Revenue grew and the largest customer grew; the share drop is mainly one lapsed account.
resolution: Already corrected before this review (the page says Ernst Handel isn't the main cause and names Piccolo und mehr). The action is now also marked tentative because the bootstrap check isn't conclusive.

objection: It uses the last 90 days, the early-1998 peak; long-run demand gives a much smaller figure.
resolution: Confirmed: the page now gives a range of 215–606 units and explains both ends.

objection: The assumption that stock was counted on 6 May 1998 should be visible in the headline.
resolution: Accepted: the key finding now states the assumption.

claim: Q2: none of the top 10 has stock on order
objection: This follows from how the tiers are defined rather than being a finding.
All were placed in the last four weeks and none is overdue, so 'holding revenue' overstates it.
resolution: Accepted: they are now described as normal work in progress and removed from the recommended actions.
